lessons.title: Layering and Glazing with Charcoal
lessons.body: Layering and glazing with charcoal means building up thin, transparent layers to create depth, richness, and subtle tonal shifts. In Africa, where dust and humidity can affect materials, you need to work with what you have. Start with a smooth paper like Canson Mi-Teintes (150 gsm) or a local equivalent. Use willow charcoal for the first layer because it erases easily. Sketch your basic shapes lightly. Then, take a soft brush or a piece of cloth and gently rub the charcoal into the paper to create a grey base. This is your first glaze. Let it settle for a minute. Next, add a second layer with compressed charcoal (like Coates or Derwent) in the darker areas. Don't press hard; just drag the side of the stick. Use a kneaded eraser to lift out highlights before adding more layers. For glazing, you can also use a bit of charcoal powder (scrape a stick with sandpaper) and apply it with a dry brush. In dry climates like the Sahel, this powder can fly, so work on a tray. In humid regions like the Congo, paper may cockle; tape it down to a board. Repeat layering: dark, then lift, then dark again. Aim for at least three layers. Each layer should be lighter than the last. This technique is great for skin tonesâthink of the deep browns and ochres of African soil. You can also use a fixative between layers (hairspray works in a pinch) to prevent smudging, but test first. Practice on a small scale: a simple sphere or a mango. Build from light to dark, then pull out highlights with a kneaded eraser. The key is patienceârushing leads to mud. With practice, you'll create drawings that look almost like paintings, with a luminous quality that flat shading can't match.

lessons.title: Subtractive Drawing
lessons.body: Subtractive drawing is the opposite of how most people start: instead of adding charcoal to white paper, you cover the paper with charcoal and then remove it to create your image. This method is perfect for dramatic effects and is very forgiving. You'll need a soft charcoal stick (like Nitram or a local brand), a soft cloth or sponge, a kneaded eraser, and a chamois. Start by covering your paperâuse a smooth or medium-textured paper like Fabriano or a locally available cartridge paper. Rub the charcoal over the entire surface, then blend it with a cloth until you have an even, dark grey or black tone. Now, use your kneaded eraser to lift out the light areas. Think of it as drawing with an eraser. For fine lines, shape the eraser into a point. For broad areas, use the flat side. You can also use a brush to sweep away charcoal dust. This technique is excellent for portraits, especially for capturing the highlights on dark skin. In Africa, where strong sunlight creates high contrast, subtractive drawing helps you show the glow of a face. Work from dark to light: first block in the darkest shadows with more charcoal if needed, then erase the mid-tones and highlights. A common mistake is erasing too much too soon. Build gradually. Use a reference photo with strong lightingâlike a portrait taken in the afternoon sun. Practice on a small scale: a single eye or a nose. You can also combine subtractive and additive methods: erase, then add more charcoal, then erase again. This back-and-forth creates rich textures. Keep a clean eraser by kneading it. In humid conditions, charcoal may smudge; work in a well-ventilated area and use a fixative at the end. With practice, you'll create drawings that have a mysterious, atmospheric quality, perfect for night scenes or dramatic portraits.

lessons.title: Combining Charcoal with Other Media
lessons.body: Charcoal doesn't have to work alone. Mixing it with other media can expand your expressive range and solve problems like smudging or lack of color. In Africa, where artists often use what's available, combining charcoal with local materials like ochre, chalk, or even coffee can create unique effects. Start with a simple combination: charcoal and white chalk on toned paper. Toned paper (like Canson Mi-Teintes in grey or tan) gives you a middle value, so you can add darks with charcoal and lights with chalk. This is fast and effective for life drawing. Another combination is charcoal and pastel. Pastel adds color and can be layered over charcoal, but be careful: pastel doesn't stick well to charcoal dust. First, fix your charcoal layer lightly. Then apply pastel in areas where you want colorâlike the red of a kanga or the blue of a sky. You can also use charcoal over a watercolor wash. Paint a light wash of watercolor (or even diluted acrylic) and let it dry completely. Then draw with charcoal on top. The charcoal will sit on the surface, and you can smudge it into the paint for soft transitions. This is great for landscapes. For a more textured look, mix charcoal with a bit of linseed oil or cooking oil to make a paste. Apply it with a brush for thick, painterly strokes. This works well on canvas or board. In dry regions, this paste dries quickly; in humid areas, it stays workable longer. You can also combine charcoal with ink. Use a dip pen or brush to add sharp black lines, then smudge charcoal around them for shadow. Experiment with what you have: charcoal and mud, charcoal and ash. The key is to test on scrap paper first. Always fix your final drawing to prevent smudging. Combining media lets you tell richer storiesâcapturing the colors of a market scene or the texture of a woven basket. Don't be afraid to mix and match.

lessons.title: Creating Dramatic Lighting
lessons.body: Dramatic lighting in charcoal drawing is about contrastâstrong darks against bright lights. This technique is essential for capturing the intense African sun, firelight, or stage lighting. To create drama, you need a clear light source and a deep shadow. Start by choosing a subject with strong directional light. A portrait lit from one side, a still life with a single candle, or a landscape at sunset. Use a soft charcoal (like willow) for the initial sketch, then switch to compressed charcoal for the darkest darks. Leave the white of the paper for the brightest highlightsâdon't cover everything. Plan your values: squint at your subject to see only three tones: light, mid-tone, and dark. Block these in with simple shapes. For the light areas, use very little charcoal or erase back to white. For mid-tones, use a light layer of charcoal, smudged. For darks, press hard with compressed charcoal. The contrast between the white paper and the black charcoal creates drama. You can also use a white pastel or chalk to add highlights on top of charcoal, especially on toned paper. In Africa, where the sun is harsh, shadows are deep and sharp. Capture that by keeping edges hard on the shadow side and soft on the light side. Use a kneaded eraser to pull out light edges. A common mistake is making the mid-tones too darkâkeep them distinct from the darks. Practice with a single object: a calabash or a face. Set up a lamp on one side. Draw the shadow shapes first, then the lights. Use a fixative between layers to prevent smudging. For night scenes, use a dark background (cover the paper with charcoal) and erase out the light. This is subtractive drawing combined with dramatic lighting. The result should feel like a spotlight. Remember, drama comes from simplicityâdon't overwork. Let the contrast speak.

lessons.title: Expressive Mark-Making
lessons.body: Expressive mark-making is about using charcoal in ways that show energy, emotion, and movementânot just smooth shading. In Africa, where art is often full of rhythm and life, this technique helps you capture the pulse of a scene. Instead of blending everything, you use visible strokes: lines, smudges, dots, and scratches. Start by experimenting with different charcoal types: willow makes light, sketchy lines; compressed charcoal makes bold, dark strokes; charcoal pencils give precise lines. Try holding the charcoal differently: use the tip for thin lines, the side for broad strokes, and the end for stamping. You can also break a stick and use the jagged edge for texture. For expressive marks, work quickly. Set a timer for 2 minutes and draw a subjectâa dancer, a tree, a market stallâusing only lines, no blending. Let your hand move freely. Use your whole arm, not just your wrist. Vary the pressure: light for distant elements, heavy for close ones. You can also use a brush to sweep charcoal dust across the paper for a smoky effect. Or dip a stick in water and drawâthis creates a dark, inky line that dries permanent. In dry climates, this dries fast; in humid areas, it stays wet longer. Combine different marks: scribbles for foliage, bold strokes for shadows, dots for texture. Don't erase mistakesâincorporate them. Expressive mark-making is about capturing the feeling of a subject, not photographic accuracy. Look at the way a baobab tree twists, or how a woman carries a potâuse angular lines for strength, curved lines for grace. Practice on large paper (A2 or bigger) so you can move freely. Use a fixative when done, as these loose marks smudge easily. This technique is perfect for sketching in the field, where speed and spontaneity matter. Let your marks tell a story.

lessons.title: Practice Project: Figure Drawing
lessons.body: This practice project brings together all the advanced techniques you've learned: layering, subtractive drawing, combining media, dramatic lighting, and expressive marks. Your goal is to draw a full figure from life or a reference photo, using charcoal as your main medium. Choose a subject that interests youâa person in a dynamic pose, like a dancer, a farmer, or a child at play. If you can't find a live model, use a photo with strong lighting. You'll need: a large sheet of paper (A2 or bigger), willow and compressed charcoal, a kneaded eraser, a chamois, and fixative. Start by planning your composition. Lightly sketch the gesture with willow charcoalâjust the basic lines of action. Spend no more than 2 minutes on this. Next, block in the major shadows using the side of a compressed charcoal stick. Don't worry about details. Now, use a chamois or cloth to smudge the charcoal into a mid-tone base. This is your first layer. Then, go back in with compressed charcoal to deepen the darkest areasâunder the chin, between the legs, in folds of clothing. Use a kneaded eraser to lift out highlights on the face, shoulders, and knees. For dramatic lighting, imagine a strong light source from one side. Keep the light side of the figure mostly paper-white, with minimal charcoal. For expressive marks, add quick lines to suggest movementâmaybe in the hair or a flowing garment. You can also combine media: add a touch of white chalk for the brightest highlights, or a bit of pastel for color in the background. Work in layers, stepping back often. Fix between layers if you need to prevent smudging. Spend about 45 minutes to an hour on this drawing. When done, sign it and fix it. This project is your chance to experiment. Don't aim for perfectionâaim for expression. After finishing, review what worked and what didn't. Try the same pose again with a different technique, like subtractive drawing. Practice makes progress.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of layering and glazing with charcoal?
options: A) To create a flat, even tone
B) To build depth and subtle tonal shifts
C) To make the drawing look like a photograph
D) To use only one type of charcoal
quiz.explanation: Layering and glazing build depth and subtle tonal shifts by applying thin, transparent layers.

quiz.q: Which charcoal type is best for the first layer in layering because it erases easily?
quiz.explanation: Willow charcoal is soft and erases easily, making it ideal for the initial layer.

quiz.q: In subtractive drawing, how do you create the image?
options: A) By adding more and more charcoal
B) By covering the paper with charcoal and then erasing
C) By using only white chalk
D) By drawing with a pen
quiz.explanation: Subtractive drawing involves covering the paper with charcoal and then removing it to create the image.

quiz.q: Which tool is essential for subtractive drawing?
quiz.explanation: A kneaded eraser is used to lift out highlights in subtractive drawing.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of combining charcoal with white chalk on toned paper?
options: A) It makes the drawing permanent
B) It provides a middle value and allows for both darks and lights
C) It eliminates the need for fixative
D) It makes the charcoal waterproof
quiz.explanation: Toned paper provides a middle value, so you can add darks with charcoal and lights with chalk.

quiz.q: When combining charcoal with pastel, what should you do first?
options: B) Fix the charcoal layer lightly
D) Use a lot of water
quiz.explanation: Fixing the charcoal layer lightly helps pastel adhere better and prevents smudging.

quiz.q: How can you create dramatic lighting in a charcoal drawing?
options: B) Use strong contrast between darks and lights
quiz.explanation: Dramatic lighting relies on strong contrast between dark shadows and bright highlights.

quiz.q: What should you leave for the brightest highlights in dramatic lighting?
options: A) The white of the paper
quiz.explanation: Leaving the white of the paper untouched creates the brightest highlights.

quiz.q: What is expressive mark-making primarily about?
options: C) Showing energy and emotion through visible strokes
D) Using only one type of mark
quiz.explanation: Expressive mark-making uses visible strokes to convey energy and emotion.

quiz.q: Which of these is an example of an expressive mark?
quiz.explanation: Scribbles are spontaneous, energetic marks that convey expression.

quiz.q: What is the first step in the practice project figure drawing?
options: A) Add details to the face
B) Sketch the gesture lightly with willow charcoal
C) Cover the paper with charcoal
quiz.explanation: Starting with a light gesture sketch helps establish the pose before adding details.

quiz.q: In the figure drawing project, how long should you spend on the initial gesture sketch?
quiz.explanation: The gesture sketch should be quick, about 2 minutes, to capture the action.

quiz.q: What is a good way to prevent smudging when layering charcoal?
options: A) Use a fixative between layers
B) Work in a humid room
quiz.explanation: A fixative between layers helps set the charcoal and prevent smudging.

quiz.q: Which paper is recommended for layering and glazing?
quiz.explanation: Canson Mi-Teintes is a smooth paper that works well for layering and glazing.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake in subtractive drawing?
options: A) Erasing too much too soon
quiz.explanation: Erasing too much too soon can remove too much tone; it's better to build gradually.

quiz.q: How can you make a charcoal paste for painting?
options: B) Mix charcoal with linseed oil
quiz.explanation: Mixing charcoal with linseed oil creates a paste that can be applied with a brush.

quiz.q: What is the benefit of using a chamois in charcoal drawing?
quiz.explanation: A chamois is used to blend charcoal into smooth transitions.

quiz.q: When creating dramatic lighting, what should you do with mid-tones?
options: A) Make them as dark as the darks
B) Keep them distinct from darks and lights
quiz.explanation: Mid-tones should be kept distinct to maintain the contrast between darks and lights.

quiz.q: Which charcoal type is best for bold, dark strokes in expressive mark-making?
quiz.explanation: Compressed charcoal is denser and produces bold, dark strokes.

quiz.q: What should you do after finishing an expressive charcoal drawing?
quiz.explanation: Fixative is needed to prevent smudging of loose expressive marks.

quiz.q: In the figure drawing project, what is the recommended time to spend on the final drawing?
quiz.explanation: Spending 45 minutes to 1 hour allows enough time to develop the drawing without overworking.

quiz.q: What is a key principle of expressive mark-making?
options: C) Use only one type of mark
quiz.explanation: Working quickly and freely helps capture energy and spontaneity.

quiz.q: Which of these is a way to create texture in charcoal drawing?
options: A) Using a brush to sweep charcoal dust
quiz.explanation: Sweeping charcoal dust with a brush creates a smoky, textured effect.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a kneaded eraser in layering?
quiz.explanation: A kneaded eraser is used to lift out highlights, creating lighter areas.

quiz.q: In subtractive drawing, what do you use to create fine lines?
options: A) The flat side of an eraser
quiz.explanation: Shaping the kneaded eraser into a point allows for fine lines.

quiz.q: What is a good subject for practicing dramatic lighting?
options: B) A portrait lit from one side
D) A still life with even lighting
quiz.explanation: A portrait lit from one side creates strong shadows and highlights, ideal for dramatic lighting.

quiz.q: When combining charcoal with watercolor, what should you do first?
options: B) Apply watercolor and let it dry
quiz.explanation: Watercolor should be applied and dried before drawing with charcoal on top.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake in expressive mark-making?
options: A) Using too many different marks
quiz.explanation: Blending too much can destroy the expressive quality of the marks.

quiz.q: In the figure drawing project, what should you do after finishing?
options: B) Fix it and review what worked
D) Show it to no one
quiz.explanation: Fixing the drawing preserves it, and reviewing helps you learn from the process.

quiz.q: Which of these is a benefit of using toned paper?
options: A) It eliminates the need for fixative
B) It provides a middle value
quiz.explanation: Toned paper provides a middle value, allowing you to work with both darks and lights.
